A.title: GoMechanic and the Valuation Trap
A.body: A fast-growing Indian auto-services startup raises multiple rounds and begins negotiating a major investment. To meet aggressive growth expectations, the leadership team speeds up month-end closes, centralizes information access, and ties bonuses to short-term revenue milestones. An internal review later reveals reporting irregularities and an overreliance on a small leadership circle for verification, even as the firm expands across cities. Investors and employees now ask whether the problem was a few ‘bad apples’ or a governance design that made misreporting predictable. As an independent director joining mid-crisis, you must decide what to fix first: incentives, monitoring, reporting controls, or board composition—and you must distinguish hidden information from hidden action when diagnosing failures. Assume any numeric details stated in the caselet are accurate for the purpose of this quiz.

B.title: FTX and the Governance Vacuum
B.body: A global crypto exchange grows rapidly and markets itself as safe, well-managed, and customer-first. Behind the scenes, internal controls are weak: the board is minimal, audits are thin, and related-party transactions are opaque. A liquidity shock triggers scrutiny and reveals that customer assets were used to support an affiliated trading firm. Regulators, auditors, and analysts are now involved, and potential acquirers circle the distressed firm. As the situation escalates, external governance mechanisms—disclosure, auditing, regulation, and the market for corporate control—become more salient than internal ones. Your task is to identify which mechanisms failed, which ones can still work, and why takeover bids can destroy value even when they ‘save’ a company. Assume any numeric details stated in the caselet are accurate for the purpose of this quiz.

C.title: VW Dieselgate and the ‘Bad Barrel’ Problem
C.body: A global automaker makes an ambitious strategic bet on a technology narrative: ‘clean diesel’ that promises performance, fuel economy, and regulatory compliance. Engineers face an ‘iron triangle’ of constraints and escalating internal pressure. A software workaround is installed that behaves differently in regulatory testing than in real-world driving. The outcome is catastrophic: investigations, fines, reputational damage, and leadership upheaval. You are asked to evaluate whether this is mainly a ‘bad apples’ story (individual intent) or a ‘bad barrel’ story (systemic pressure, incentives, and tone at the top). You must also separate what was legal from what was ethical, and propose governance and culture interventions that are credible rather than symbolic. Assume any numeric details stated in the caselet are accurate for the purpose of this quiz.

D.title: Country Delight, D-Mart, and Business Model Precision
D.body: A consumer brand scales by promising freshness and trust in a fragmented supply chain. It uses a subscription model to forecast demand, reduce spoilage, and deliver directly to homes. At the same time, the company experiments with adjacent offers: bundles, memberships, and private-label add-ons. Investors debate whether the ‘strategy’ is clear or whether the firm is just stacking tactics. Meanwhile, a leading discount retailer wins on everyday low cost and everyday low price through ownership choices and working-capital discipline. Your job is to use the business-model framework (why–what–who–how) to diagnose which moves strengthen unit economics, which create lock-in, and which are likely to backfire by raising complexity without creating value. Assume any numeric details stated in the caselet are accurate for the purpose of this quiz.

A.title: BYD’s Europe dilemma under anti-subsidy tariffs
A.body:
In mid-2024 the European Union moved to impose provisional countervailing duties on battery-electric vehicles imported from China, with company-specific rates (on top of the EU’s standard car import duty). The move raised the effective landed cost of China-built EVs and increased policy volatility for Chinese brands expanding in Europe. BYD’s response was not only commercial (pricing, dealer networks) but structural: it announced a new passenger-car manufacturing base in Szeged, Hungary, positioning it as localised European production and a longer-term hedge against tariff escalation and regulatory scrutiny. 

For strategy, the interesting question is not “tariffs bad, local factory good.” It is subtler: which ‘distance’ is being reduced (and which may increase), whether the investment is the right foreign-entry mode given control and capital intensity, and how BYD should navigate the competing pressures for cost reduction and local responsiveness across a multi-country European market.

Sources (for the caselet facts): Reuters on EU provisional duties (July 2024); BYD press release on the Hungary plant (Dec 2023).

B.title: Apple’s “China + 1” pivot, but with frictions
B.body:
Apple has accelerated its effort to diversify iPhone assembly away from China by expanding production in India with partners such as Foxconn and Tata. Reports in 2024 suggested India’s share of iPhone output had risen sharply, while 2025 reporting described Apple holding urgent talks to produce most U.S.-bound iPhones in India to reduce tariff exposure and geopolitical risk. Yet the move is not frictionless: analysts note India assembly can be costlier than China and that much of the component ecosystem remains China-centric; some reporting also pointed to regulatory and logistical roadblocks affecting equipment movement. 

For global strategy, the puzzle is deliberately uncomfortable: the same move can look like ‘location economies’ (better risk-adjusted costs), a response to ‘administrative distance’ (tariffs, export controls), and an attempt to manage systemic rivalry—while simultaneously raising coordination costs and new liabilities of foreignness in operations and workforce ecosystems.

Sources (for the caselet facts): CNBC on Apple’s India output shift (Apr 2024); Reuters reporting (Apr 2025, via Reuters video/Al Jazeera summary) on accelerating U.S.-bound assembly to India.

C.title: Shein’s globalization: scale, scrutiny, and ‘administrative distance’
C.body:
Shein built a global fast-fashion machine on cross-border e-commerce, data-driven trend detection, and a supplier base deeply tied to China. But when it pursued a London IPO, it encountered a layered regulatory stack: UK listing approval was only one gate; Chinese offshore-listing rules and political scrutiny over supply-chain practices created additional frictions. At the same time, policy shifts in major markets—such as changes to low-value shipment treatment and new tariff regimes—threatened the economics of ultra-low-cost cross-border fulfillment. Shein’s reported response included supplier diversification (e.g., toward Brazil and Turkey), a signal that “distance” in global strategy is not just geography but also politics, institutions, and reputational exposure.

For students, the uncomfortable diagnostic is: which entry and operating choices reduce administrative distance but raise other distances? And when does a firm’s global strategy shift from ‘export-like’ cross-border selling toward deeper, more investment-intensive local operations?

Sources (for the caselet facts): Reuters on Shein’s London IPO approvals and pending China clearance (Apr 2025).

D.title: Nvidia in a techno cold war: ‘where to sell’ becomes ‘what can be shipped’
D.body:
Nvidia’s AI accelerators became a strategic choke point in U.S.–China competition. As U.S. export controls tightened, Nvidia repeatedly adjusted its China-facing product line, and reporting in early 2026 described the firm stopping production of a China-intended chip variant amid uncertainty over approvals and restrictions. At the policy level, Reuters reporting in March 2026 described U.S. officials considering new export-rule designs for AI chips, potentially extending compliance conditions even to allies via security guarantees and monitoring requirements.

This creates a distinctive global-strategy exam setting: the firm’s challenge is not only customer demand and competitor rivalry. It is administrative distance weaponised—trade rules and security logic that reshape which markets are ‘enterable,’ what entry modes remain available, and how to balance cost efficiency with local responsiveness when ‘local’ includes government constraints.

Sources (for the caselet facts): Financial Times on Nvidia halting China-intended chip production (Mar 2026); Reuters on proposed U.S. AI chip export-rule framework (Mar 2026).
